title: La ce, la zeta, la jota y la eñe
summary: The Castilian 'th' sound (distinción), the jota, and ñ / ll / rr

blocks.title: The Castilian 'th' — distinción
blocks.body: In Spain, **z** and **c before e or i** are pronounced like the **th in 'think'** (a soft lisp, tongue between the teeth): *gracias, cinco, plaza, zapato*. This is called **distinción**, and it's one of the clearest markers of Spain Spanish. In Latin America these all sound like 's' — here, they don't.

pairs.note: *cena* and *zapato* start with the same 'th' sound. Spanish just spells it c before e/i, z elsewhere.

blocks.title: The jota — that throat scrape
blocks.body: The letter **j** (and **g before e or i**) is a rough sound made at the back of the throat, like clearing it: *jamón, Juan, gente, Madrid* (the *d*-*rid* has a soft *g*-like scrape too in *general*). Think of the 'ch' in Scottish 'loch'. Don't be shy — it's meant to rasp.
blocks.callout: *g* before a/o/u is a normal hard g (*gato, gustar*); only *ge/gi* get the scrape (*gente, gitano*).

blocks.prompt: How does a Spaniard pronounce the c in *cerveza*?
blocks.explain: c before e/i = /θ/, the 'th' sound. And there's a z in there too — *cer-**ve**-za* has the 'th' twice. Distinción in one glorious word for beer.

blocks.title: ñ, ll and the rolled rr
blocks.body: Three more sounds: **ñ** = 'ny' as in 'canyon' (*España, niño, año*); **ll** = a 'y' sound in most of Spain (*llave, calle, paella*); **rr** is a **rolled/trilled r** (*perro, arroz*). A single *r* between vowels is a soft tap (*pero*); double *rr* is the full roll — and it changes meaning: *pero* (but) vs *perro* (dog).
blocks.callout: Can't roll the rr yet? Nobody rolls it on day 2. Tap it for now, keep practising.

blocks.explain: *perro* (dog) has the rolled *rr*; *pero* (but) has a single soft *r*. The roll carries the meaning.

blocks.prompt: Listen and type what you hear.
Which sound felt hardest — the 'th', the jota, or the rolled rr? Type two words with each of the sounds you want to nail this week.
